analysis.one_liner: Gives working parents of young children a $6,000 refundable tax credit, paid out monthly.
analysis.headline: A bill to give parents a $6,000 refundable tax credit ($12,000 per couple) was sent to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2021, drew zero cosponsors, and never received a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a new refundable tax credit of $6,000 per parent ($12,000 per married couple) for anyone with a child under 13, sent in monthly installments instead of a once-a-year refund. It would only go to parents who earn at least the federal minimum wage times 1,040 hours (about $7,500 a year), and it would repeal the existing tax credit for child and dependent care expenses. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there without ever being taken up.
analysis.who_benefits: Working parents with children under 13 would gain a large cash benefit — $6,000 per parent per year, fully refundable, delivered monthly, adjusted for inflation after 2022, and protected from being seized to pay back taxes or other federal debts [S2] [S3]. The credit would be flat, with no phase-down at higher incomes, so middle- and upper-income parents would get the full amount too. A special rule would let military spouses with limited identification paperwork still qualify [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Parents earning at least $7,500 a year

how_it_helps.text: Gives parents of children under 13 a refundable credit of $6,000 ($12,000 on a joint return), meaning families owing little or no income tax would still receive the money.

Requires the IRS to send the credit in monthly advance payments during the year, the same structure used for the 2021 expanded child tax credit, so families get the money when bills come due rather than at tax time.
The credit cannot be reduced or offset to collect back federal taxes, student loans, or other federal debts, so families with tax problems keep the full amount.
The $6,000 and $12,000 amounts would rise with inflation each year beginning after 2022, so the benefit would not shrink in real terms.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, since the bill includes no offsetting revenue and would add roughly $6,000 times the number of eligible parents per year to the deficit [S3]. Families who rely on the existing child and dependent care tax credit to help pay for child care would also lose that credit, since the bill repeals it after 2021 [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; families using the child care credit

drawbacks.text: The credit requires earned income of at least the federal minimum wage times 1,040 hours — about $7,540 a year — so parents with no or very low earnings, including stay-at-home parents and those unable to work, would get nothing.

It repeals the child and dependent care tax credit after 2021, which specifically helps working families pay for child care; a family could gain the parent credit but lose the credit tied to its largest expense.
The bill contains no revenue offsets, so the full cost would be added to the federal deficit.

Parents who receive monthly advance payments and then fall below the earnings floor would lose the credit and be barred from advance payments for the next two years, with the credit cut in half during that period.
The credit does not phase out at higher incomes, so even the highest-earning parents would receive the full $6,000, which raises the cost per dollar of help delivered to families who need it most.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — several thousand dollars a year, paid monthly, to working families with young children — would be substantial and immediate. But the design carries real costs: no offsetting revenue, a full credit for the wealthiest parents, an earnings floor that excludes parents without jobs, and the repeal of the child care credit that many two-earner families depend on. An honest supporter would call it a generous but expensive and imperfectly targeted proposal; the cost of the flat credit for all income levels is the biggest weakness.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing, markup, or vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Josh Hawley introduced the bill on April 28, 2021; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
The bill never attracted a single cosponsor during its entire two-year life in the Senate.
No further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — appears in the record before Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained directly, but taxpayers were spared an unoffset cost, families using the child and dependent care credit kept it, and the existing child tax credit structure was left unchanged. Parents of young children, who would have received the monthly payments, are the ones who lost out.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers and child-care-credit users; parents lost out

for.name: Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Parent Tax Credit Act and was its only sponsor; no other senator joined.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from April 2021 until the Congress ended, taking no hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee of jurisdiction, never scheduled the bill for consideration during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and no party bloc ever took a position; the bill had one Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party.

industries.note: The bill repeals the child and dependent care tax credit after 2021, which subsidizes families' child care spending. Providers would face families with less help paying for care, a loss shared with the families themselves.
The bill creates a large entitlement with no offsetting revenue, adding to deficits. Individual taxpayers would gain from the credit but bear the cost collectively.
